headline: Flash-panning: romance that starts hot and ends in silence

sources.title: Flashpanning Is Yet Another Troubling Dating Trend Fueled By Commitment-Phobes (Glam)
Dating expert reveals how flashpanning works (video, USA TODAY)

chunks.text: It starts like a movie. Two people meet online and {{hit it off}} so well that they text all night and see each other every day. There are flowers, long walks, and big [[promises]]. She is [[swept off her feet]] and {{falls for}} him completely. The new [[couple]] even {{show off}} the [[romance]] online, where every photo looks like a [[perfect match]]. Dating experts call this [[pattern]] [[flash-panning]], and it has a [[cruel]] ending.

verbs.correct: To like each other right away
verbs.wrong: To argue from the first day
verbs.why: Two strangers can hit it off at a party, and new coworkers sometimes hit it off on the very first day. This couple hit it off so well that they were texting all night and seeing each other daily.

People fall for a kind smile, and sometimes they fall for someone before they really know that person. She fell for him quickly, charmed by flowers, long walks, and big promises before ordinary life began.
Kids show off a new bike to friends, and travelers show off vacation photos online. This couple showed off their romance online, where every picture looked like a perfect match.

chunks.text: Then [[ordinary]] life {{comes along}}: work schedules, tired evenings, and small [[disagreements]]. For most couples, this is where real love begins. For a flashpanner, it is the [[exit]]. The excitement {{wears off}}, and he begins {{pulling away}}, answering less and less each day. Soon he disappears completely, without a fight and without an [[explanation]]. The person {{left behind}} keeps asking the same question: what did I do wrong?

verbs.why: A good opportunity can come along when you least expect it, and sometimes trouble comes along just as things feel settled. Here ordinary life comes along, with work schedules, tired evenings, and small disagreements.
The excitement of a new job can wear off after a few months, and the thrill of new shoes can wear off after one wear. For a flashpanner, the early excitement wears off the moment real life starts.

In relationships, a partner can pull away when things start to feel too serious, and a friend might pull away after an argument. He starts pulling away by answering her messages less and less each day.

verbs.correct: To go and not take someone with you
verbs.wrong: To carry someone a long way
verbs.why: A fast hiker can leave behind slower friends on a trail, and a careless traveler might leave behind a bag at the airport. A flashpanner disappears completely and leaves the other person behind, confused and hurt.

chunks.text: Why do people do this? Relationship expert Susan Winter says flashpanners love the [[electric]] first weeks but cannot {{deal with}} boring Tuesdays and real [[compromise]]. Many never learned that small fights are a normal part of love, and some are afraid to {{open up}} about their deeper feelings. The pattern is not new: a radio show described it back in 2019. It is also different from [[ghosting]], which usually happens after little contact, and from [[love bombing]], where [[extreme]] attention is used for [[control]].

verbs.why: Nurses deal with stress every shift, and parents deal with tantrums calmly. Flashpanners love the exciting first weeks but cannot deal with boring Tuesdays and the compromise real love needs.

verbs.wrong: To make a joke of something
verbs.why: Close friends open up about their fears late at night, and therapy helps some people open up for the first time. Some flashpanners never open up, because closeness itself makes them nervous.

chunks.text: The harm is real. After weeks of [[closeness]], the sudden silence can feel like losing a friend, and it can take months to {{get over}} someone who simply disappeared. Experts say the best [[defense]] is a little [[patience]]. So {{watch out for}} the [[warning signs]]: a [[flawless]] first week, gifts and big promises, and [[excitement]] that feels too strong too soon. Real love grows more slowly, and it survives boring Tuesdays.

verbs.correct: To feel better after something bad
verbs.why: It takes time to get over a bad cold, and some people never fully get over their first heartbreak. It can take months to get over someone who disappeared without any explanation.

verbs.correct: To be careful about a danger
verbs.why: Drivers watch out for ice on the road, and shoppers watch out for hidden fees on cheap deals. Experts say to watch out for a perfect first week, early gifts, and promises that feel too big too soon.

mainIdea.s: Flash-panning is a dating pattern where someone starts a romance with great energy and then disappears when ordinary life begins. Experts say daters should learn the signs.
mainIdea.why: The article describes an intense start, then a sudden exit when schedules and small disagreements arrive.

mainIdea.s: In a pattern called flash-panning, people give new partners extreme attention in order to control them for years. Experts now say it is simply another name for love bombing.
mainIdea.why: Close, but flashpanners leave when things get real. The article says love bombing is a different pattern, used for control.

mainIdea.s: A dating app added a tool this year that warns users when a new match sends too many messages too quickly. Millions of daters have already turned the new warning on.
mainIdea.why: No app tool appears in the article. It is about a dating pattern and its warning signs.

tf.s: In a flash-panning romance, the first days are quiet and slow
tf.why: The start is intense. The two people hit it off fast, with constant dates, texts, and big promises.

tf.s: Flashpanners often pull away when everyday problems come along
tf.why: When schedules and small disagreements appear, the excitement wears off and they start to disappear.

tf.s: The expert says many flashpanners never learned that small fights are normal in love
tf.why: She says they cannot deal with the boring days and compromise that real relationships need.

tf.s: The article says flash-panning and ghosting are exactly the same thing
tf.why: Ghosting usually happens after little contact. Flash-panning starts with weeks of closeness first.

tf.s: The advice is to watch out for a romance that feels perfect from day one
tf.why: A flawless first week, early gifts, and big promises can be warning signs.

tf.s: The term flash-panning was invented this summer
tf.why: A radio show described the pattern back in 2019, but it is getting fresh attention now.
